items.stem: What is meant by marginal utility?
options: Total utility divided by the number of units consumed
The price a consumer pays for the last unit bought
The additional satisfaction gained from consuming one more unit of a good
The total satisfaction gained from all units consumed
items.answer: The additional satisfaction gained from consuming one more unit of a good
items.markingKey: Marginal utility = change in total utility from one extra unit consumed (ΔTU/ΔQ).

items.stem: Explain how the law of diminishing marginal utility helps to explain why an individual demand curve slopes downwards.
items.answer: A consumer buys a unit only if its marginal utility (in money terms) is at least its price. Because MU falls as more is consumed, the consumer will only buy extra units if the price falls, so quantity demanded rises as price falls.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: consumer buys while MU ≥ P (or MU/P equalised); 1 mark: MU falls with extra units; 1 mark: so more units bought only at lower price, giving a downward-sloping demand curve [3]

items.stem: Explain the paradox of value (the diamonds–water paradox) using the distinction between total and marginal utility.
items.answer: Water has a very high total utility but, because it is plentiful, the marginal utility of the last unit consumed is low, so its price is low. Diamonds are scarce, so the marginal utility of the last unit is high and so is the price. Price reflects marginal, not total, utility.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: water high TU, diamonds low TU; 1 mark: water abundant so low MU; 1 mark: price is linked to MU, not TU [3]

items.stem: The table shows a consumer’s total utility. Units of airline seats consumed per week: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Total utility (utils): 60, 117, 169, 217, 260, 295. Calculate the marginal utility of unit 4.
items.answer: 48 utils

items.stem: The table shows a consumer’s total utility. Units of bus journeys consumed per week: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Total utility (utils): 36, 66, 93, 112, 126, 122. Calculate the marginal utility of unit 2.
items.answer: 30 utils

items.stem: Consumers in Selmaria are spending more of their rising incomes on streaming subscriptions. To what extent do you agree that price reflects marginal utility rather than total utility, so essential goods are usually cheap?
items.answer: Arguments for: Price depends on MU of the last unit; plentiful goods (water) have low MU and low prices despite high TU; scarce goods (diamonds) have high MU. Arguments against / evaluation: Price is also set by supply and costs; essential goods can be expensive when scarce (medicines, housing); market power and information gaps distort prices. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: Explain why total utility can still be increasing when marginal utility is falling.
items.answer: As long as marginal utility is positive, each extra unit adds something to total utility, so total utility rises, but by smaller amounts each time.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: MU positive means TU rises; 1 mark: falling MU means TU rises at a decreasing rate [2]

items.stem: Explain why marginal utility theory assumes that utility is cardinal and why this is a weakness.
items.answer: Marginal utility theory measures satisfaction in units (utils) that can be added and compared, so it assumes utility is cardinal. In practice satisfaction is subjective and cannot be measured or compared numerically between people.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: cardinal = measurable in units/utils; 1 mark: satisfaction subjective, cannot be measured [2]

items.stem: The table shows a consumer’s total utility, where 1 util is worth $1 to the consumer. Units of smartphones consumed per week: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Total utility (utils): 60, 115, 165, 210, 252, 289. The price is $55 per unit. Calculate how many units a rational consumer buys and explain your answer.
items.answer: 2 units
items.markingKey: MU of each unit: 60, 55, 50, 45, 42, 37. Buy every unit whose MU ≥ price ($55) → 2 units [2]; the next unit has MU 50 < price [1].

items.stem: The table shows a consumer’s total utility. Units of smartphones consumed per week: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Total utility (utils): 36, 68, 92, 113, 128, 138. Calculate the marginal utility of unit 4.
items.answer: 21 utils

items.answer: (a) 3 units (b) $13

items.stem: A consumer with a fixed income maximises total utility from two goods, A and B, when
options: the price of A equals the price of B
MU of A = MU of B
total utility from A equals total utility from B
MU of A ÷ price of A = MU of B ÷ price of B
items.answer: MU of A ÷ price of A = MU of B ÷ price of B
items.markingKey: Equi-marginal principle: marginal utility per dollar is equal for all goods, with all income spent.

items.stem: Explain, using the equi-marginal principle, how a fall in the price of one good leads to a higher quantity demanded of that good.
items.answer: Initially MU/P is equal across goods. A fall in the price of X raises MU(X)/P(X), so the consumer gains more utility per dollar from X and switches spending towards it. As more X is consumed its MU falls until MU(X)/P(X) is again equal to the ratio for other goods, at a higher quantity of X.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: initial equality; 1 mark: price fall raises MU/P for X; 1 mark: buy more X until MU falls and ratios equal [3]

items.stem: Explain why a consumer who spends all their income does not necessarily maximise utility.
items.answer: Spending all income is necessary but not sufficient: utility is only maximised if the last dollar spent on each good gives the same marginal utility. If MU/P differs, reallocating spending raises total utility.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: equal MU/P condition; 1 mark: reallocation raises TU if ratios differ [2]

items.stem: A consumer is in equilibrium buying cinema tickets and laptops. The marginal utility of the last unit of cinema tickets is 25 utils and its price is $5. The marginal utility of the last unit of laptops is 30 utils. Calculate the price of laptops.

A consumer is in equilibrium buying bottled water and restaurant meals. The marginal utility of the last unit of bottled water is 12 utils and its price is $2. The marginal utility of the last unit of restaurant meals is 24 utils. Calculate the price of restaurant meals.

A consumer has $12 a week to spend on textbooks (price $4) and bottled water (price $1). Units: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; MU of textbooks (utils): 28, 24, 20, 16, 12, 8; MU of bottled water (utils): 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4. Calculate the combination of the two goods that maximises the consumer’s total utility and show that the equi-marginal condition holds. Then explain what would happen to the consumer’s purchases if the price of textbooks fell, other things equal.
items.answer: 2 units of textbooks and 4 units of bottled water; MU/P = 6 for both and spending = $12. A fall in the price of textbooks raises MU/P for textbooks, so more textbooks is bought (a downward-sloping demand curve).
items.markingKey: MU/P for textbooks: 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2; for bottled water: 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4 [1]. Equal ratio (6) at 2 of textbooks and 4 of bottled water [1]; cost 2×4 + 4×1 = $12 = income [1]. Price fall raises MU/P for the good; buy more until MU falls and ratios equalise [2].

items.stem: Prices of bottled water in Umbria Nova have fallen sharply while incomes are unchanged. (a) Explain the equi-marginal principle and how it leads a consumer to an equilibrium. (b) Assess whether the equi-marginal principle is an accurate description of how consumers allocate their income.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Consumers equalise MU per dollar across goods, spending all income; a price change disturbs the equality and changes the bundle. (b) Case for the view: Consumers equalise MU per dollar across goods, spending all income; a price change disturbs the equality and changes the bundle. Case against / evaluation: Consumers rarely calculate; bounded rationality, habit, imperfect information and indivisible goods; yet the model predicts the direction of responses to price changes well. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: If MU(A)/P(A) is greater than MU(B)/P(B), a utility-maximising consumer should
options: buy equal quantities of both goods
buy more of B and less of A
buy more of A and less of B
items.answer: buy more of A and less of B
items.markingKey: The last dollar gives more satisfaction spent on A; switching raises TU until the ratios are equal.

items.stem: Distinguish between the equi-marginal principle and the law of diminishing marginal utility.
items.answer: Diminishing MU describes how satisfaction from extra units of one good falls; the equi-marginal principle is the rule for allocating a budget across goods so that MU per dollar is equal for all goods. The second relies on the first.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each definition; 1 mark link: diminishing MU makes the equalisation possible [3]

items.stem: Freya spends a weekly budget on rice and bicycles. The marginal utility per dollar from rice is higher than from bicycles. Explain what Freya should do and why.
items.answer: Switch spending from bicycles to rice. Each dollar moved raises total utility because it buys more satisfaction. As more rice is bought its MU falls and as less bicycles is bought its MU rises, until MU per dollar is equal.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: buy more rice, less bicycles; 1 mark: diminishing MU brings ratios into equality [2]

items.stem: A consumer has $19 a week to spend on cement (price $5) and smartphones (price $3). Units: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; MU of cement (utils): 30, 25, 20, 15, 10, 5; MU of smartphones (utils): 21, 18, 15, 12, 9, 6. Calculate the combination of the two goods that maximises the consumer’s total utility and show that the equi-marginal condition holds.
items.answer: 2 units of cement and 3 units of smartphones; MU/P = 5 for both and spending = $19.
items.markingKey: MU/P for cement: 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1; for smartphones: 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 [1]. Equal ratio (5) at 2 of cement and 3 of smartphones [1]; cost 2×5 + 3×3 = $19 = income [1].

items.answer: 4 units of airline seats and 2 units of chocolate bars; MU/P = 6 for both and spending = $14.
items.markingKey: MU/P for airline seats: 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4; for chocolate bars: 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 [1]. Equal ratio (6) at 4 of airline seats and 2 of chocolate bars [1]; cost 4×2 + 2×3 = $14 = income [1].

items.stem: A consumer values each util at $1. The marginal utility of successive units of laptops is 24, 19, 11, 3, -1, -5 utils. Calculate the quantity demanded at a price of $18 and at $2, and explain how these points relate to the consumer’s demand curve.
items.answer: 2 units at $18; 4 units at $2. These are two points on a downward-sloping individual demand curve.
items.markingKey: Buy units with MU ≥ P: at $18, 2 units [1]; at $2, 4 units [1]; the lower price gives the higher quantity because MU diminishes, tracing the demand curve [1].

items.stem: Which concept describes consumers making decisions that are “good enough” because of limited information and time?
items.answer: Bounded rationality
items.markingKey: Bounded rationality: decision-making limited by information, cognitive ability and time.

items.stem: A shop displays a “recommended price” of $120 next to its selling price of $80. Which behavioural idea is it using?
items.answer: Anchoring
items.markingKey: Anchoring: consumers judge value relative to a reference figure presented first.

items.stem: Explain two reasons why consumers may not behave in the way predicted by marginal utility theory.
items.answer: Consumers have imperfect information about products and prices; decisions are often made by habit or on impulse rather than by calculation; consumers are influenced by others (herd behaviour) and by how choices are framed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Shoppers in Kathmandu choose the first acceptable mobile phone contract rather than comparing all 40 contracts available. Which behavioural concept best explains this?
items.answer: Bounded rationality
items.markingKey: Bounded rationality: the situation departs from the rational consumer model in exactly this way.

items.stem: Consider whether behavioural economics has shown that the traditional model of the rational consumer is of little use.
items.answer: Arguments for: Behavioural insights (bounded rationality, anchoring, defaults, herd behaviour, bounded self-control) show systematic departures from rational choice. Arguments against / evaluation: The traditional model still predicts average responses to price changes and is simple; behavioural effects vary across contexts; best seen as complementary. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.

items.stem: Explain what is meant by bounded self-control and give an example.
items.answer: Bounded self-control is where people know what is best for them in the long run but lack the willpower to do it, e.g. intending to save but spending on impulse, or overeating despite wanting to lose weight.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: meaning; 1 mark: example [2]

items.stem: The law of diminishing marginal utility states that, as consumption of a good increases,
options: total utility falls from the first unit
each additional unit eventually adds less to total utility than the previous unit
the price of the good falls
items.answer: each additional unit eventually adds less to total utility than the previous unit
items.markingKey: With other consumption held constant, MU of successive units eventually falls.

items.stem: Explain why a buffet restaurant in Auckland can charge a single price yet expect most diners to stop eating long before they have eaten all the food on offer.
items.answer: Once the meal is paid for, the marginal price of extra food is zero, so diners eat until marginal utility falls to zero. Because marginal utility diminishes quickly, this happens after a limited number of plates.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: marginal price zero so eat until MU = 0; 1 mark: diminishing MU limits consumption [2]

items.markingKey: Lower P raises MU per dollar for X; consumer buys more X until MU(X) falls and ratios are equal again: a downward-sloping demand curve.

items.stem: Enrolling workers into a pension scheme automatically unless they opt out is an example of
options: a nudge using a default choice
items.answer: a nudge using a default choice
items.markingKey: Default options exploit inertia: changing the default changes behaviour without restricting choice.

items.stem: Explain how a government might use a “nudge” to reduce sugar consumption without banning sugary drinks.
items.answer: It could change choice architecture, for example requiring healthy drinks to be placed at eye level and sugary drinks less visibly, using clear traffic-light labels or setting water as the default drink with meals. Choice is preserved but the easiest option becomes the healthier one.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: definition of nudge (choice architecture, freedom kept); 1 mark: developed example [2]

items.stem: Northwind in Sundara changed its pension scheme from “opt in” to automatic enrolment with the right to opt out. Participation among its 2,000 workers rose from 45% to 82%. Explain why this result is difficult to explain using the model of the rational consumer.
items.answer: A rational consumer would join if the benefits exceeded costs whatever the default; the large change shows inertia and the power of defaults (status quo bias).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: rational model predicts no change; 1 mark: default/inertia explanation [2]

items.stem: A study in Marvona found that most shoppers could not recall the price of goods they had just bought. (a) Explain, with examples, what is meant by a nudge. (b) Assess whether governments should use nudges rather than taxes to change consumer behaviour.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Nudges keep freedom of choice, are cheap and can overcome bounded self-control (defaults, framing, placement). (b) Case for the view: Nudges keep freedom of choice, are cheap and can overcome bounded self-control (defaults, framing, placement). Case against / evaluation: Effects may be small or temporary; taxes give a reliable price signal and raise revenue; nudges can be manipulative; mix of measures likely best, depending on the scale of the problem. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.

items.answer: zero
items.markingKey: TU peaks where the next unit adds nothing: MU = 0.

items.stem: Explain why a buffet restaurant in Dubai can charge a single price yet expect most diners to stop eating long before they have eaten all the food on offer.
items.answer: Once the meal is paid for, the marginal price of extra food is zero, so diners eat until marginal utility falls to zero. Because marginal utility diminishes quickly, this happens after a limited number of plates.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: marginal price zero so eat until MU = 0; 1 mark: diminishing MU limits consumption [2]

items.stem: Noah buys rice every week. Explain, using the concept of marginal utility, why Noah is unlikely to buy many more units of rice even if their income rises a little.
items.answer: Each additional unit gives less extra satisfaction than the last, so beyond a point the marginal utility of an extra unit falls below its price; Noah prefers to spend extra income on other goods with a higher MU per dollar.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: diminishing MU of extra units; 1 mark: compares MU with price / MU per dollar of other goods [2]

items.stem: The table shows a consumer’s total utility. Units of bottled water consumed per week: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Total utility (utils): 50, 96, 136, 168, 194, 216. Calculate the marginal utility of unit 4.
items.answer: 32 utils

items.stem: The table shows a consumer’s total utility, where 1 util is worth $1 to the consumer. Units of smartphones consumed per week: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Total utility (utils): 60, 116, 169, 216, 257, 295. The price is $46 per unit. Calculate how many units a rational consumer buys and explain your answer.
items.answer: 4 units
items.markingKey: MU of each unit: 60, 56, 53, 47, 41, 38. Buy every unit whose MU ≥ price ($46) → 4 units [2]; the next unit has MU 41 < price [1].

items.stem: Consumers in Valdoria are spending more of their rising incomes on coffee. Assess whether price reflects marginal utility rather than total utility, so essential goods are usually cheap.
items.answer: Arguments for: Price depends on MU of the last unit; plentiful goods (water) have low MU and low prices despite high TU; scarce goods (diamonds) have high MU. Arguments against / evaluation: Price is also set by supply and costs; essential goods can be expensive when scarce (medicines, housing); market power and information gaps distort prices. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: The equi-marginal principle assumes that consumers
options: are rational and aim to maximise utility with full information
aim to maximise the number of goods bought
items.answer: are rational and aim to maximise utility with full information
items.markingKey: Assumptions: rationality, utility maximisation, known prices and MU, given income and tastes.

items.stem: Mei spends a weekly budget on bottled water and printed newspapers. The marginal utility per dollar from bottled water is higher than from printed newspapers. Explain what Mei should do and why.
items.answer: Switch spending from printed newspapers to bottled water. Each dollar moved raises total utility because it buys more satisfaction. As more bottled water is bought its MU falls and as less printed newspapers is bought its MU rises, until MU per dollar is equal.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: buy more bottled water, less printed newspapers; 1 mark: diminishing MU brings ratios into equality [2]

items.stem: Chloe spends a weekly budget on bicycles and bottled water. The marginal utility per dollar from bicycles is higher than from bottled water. Explain what Chloe should do and why.
items.answer: Switch spending from bottled water to bicycles. Each dollar moved raises total utility because it buys more satisfaction. As more bicycles is bought its MU falls and as less bottled water is bought its MU rises, until MU per dollar is equal.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: buy more bicycles, less bottled water; 1 mark: diminishing MU brings ratios into equality [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why a consumer who spends all their income does not necessarily maximise utility. (b) Distinguish between the equi-marginal principle and the law of diminishing marginal utility.
items.answer: (a) Spending all income is necessary but not sufficient: utility is only maximised if the last dollar spent on each good gives the same marginal utility. If MU/P differs, reallocating spending raises total utility. (b) Diminishing MU describes how satisfaction from extra units of one good falls; the equi-marginal principle is the rule for allocating a budget across goods so that MU per dollar is equal for all goods. The second relies on the first.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: equal MU/P condition; 1 mark: reallocation raises TU if ratios differ [2] (b) 1 mark each definition; 1 mark link: diminishing MU makes the equalisation possible [3]

items.stem: A consumer has $15 a week to spend on rice (price $1) and running shoes (price $3). Units: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; MU of rice (utils): 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3; MU of running shoes (utils): 27, 24, 21, 18, 15, 12. Calculate the combination of the two goods that maximises the consumer’s total utility and show that the equi-marginal condition holds.
items.answer: 3 units of rice and 4 units of running shoes; MU/P = 6 for both and spending = $15.
items.markingKey: MU/P for rice: 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3; for running shoes: 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4 [1]. Equal ratio (6) at 3 of rice and 4 of running shoes [1]; cost 3×1 + 4×3 = $15 = income [1].

items.stem: A consumer values each util at $1. The marginal utility of successive units of bus journeys is 40, 34, 26, 23, 17, 14 utils. Calculate the quantity demanded at a price of $34 and at $22, and explain how these points relate to the consumer’s demand curve.
items.answer: 2 units at $34; 4 units at $22. These are two points on a downward-sloping individual demand curve.
items.markingKey: Buy units with MU ≥ P: at $34, 2 units [1]; at $22, 4 units [1]; the lower price gives the higher quantity because MU diminishes, tracing the demand curve [1].

items.stem: A consumer is in equilibrium buying electric scooters and chocolate bars. The marginal utility of the last unit of electric scooters is 36 utils and its price is $6. The marginal utility of the last unit of chocolate bars is 6 utils. Calculate the price of chocolate bars.

Prices of bus journeys in Kestria have fallen sharply while incomes are unchanged. (a) Explain the equi-marginal principle and how it leads a consumer to an equilibrium. (b) Consider whether the equi-marginal principle is an accurate description of how consumers allocate their income.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Consumers equalise MU per dollar across goods, spending all income; a price change disturbs the equality and changes the bundle. (b) Case for the view: Consumers equalise MU per dollar across goods, spending all income; a price change disturbs the equality and changes the bundle. Case against / evaluation: Consumers rarely calculate; bounded rationality, habit, imperfect information and indivisible goods; yet the model predicts the direction of responses to price changes well. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.answer: Arguments for: Consumers equalise MU per dollar across goods, spending all income; a price change disturbs the equality and changes the bundle. Arguments against / evaluation: Consumers rarely calculate; bounded rationality, habit, imperfect information and indivisible goods; yet the model predicts the direction of responses to price changes well. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.

items.stem: Buying a product mainly because many other people are buying it is called
items.answer: herd behaviour
items.markingKey: Herd behaviour: imitating others’ choices.

items.stem: Explain why consumers might value a $50 loss more highly than a $50 gain.
items.answer: Loss aversion: people feel the pain of a loss more strongly than the pleasure of an equal gain, so their behaviour is asymmetric, contradicting the assumption that utility depends only on final outcomes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: loss aversion; 1 mark: contradicts rational model [2]

items.stem: Shoppers in Santiago choose the first acceptable mobile phone contract rather than comparing all 40 contracts available. Which behavioural concept best explains this?
items.answer: Bounded rationality
items.markingKey: Bounded rationality: the situation departs from the rational consumer model in exactly this way.

items.stem: Borealis plc in Istrana changed its pension scheme from “opt in” to automatic enrolment with the right to opt out. Participation among its 1,500 workers rose from 49% to 86%. (a) Calculate how many more workers joined the scheme. (b) Explain why this result is difficult to explain using the model of the rational consumer.
items.answer: (a) 555 workers (b) A rational consumer would join if the benefits exceeded costs whatever the default; the large change shows inertia and the power of defaults (status quo bias).
items.markingKey: (a) 1,500 × 37% = 555 [1] (b) 1 mark: rational model predicts no change; 1 mark: default/inertia explanation [2]

items.stem: The government of Pelora is concerned about rising obesity and low household saving. (a) Explain, with examples, what is meant by a nudge. (b) ‘Governments should use nudges rather than taxes to change consumer behaviour.’ Discuss this view.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Nudges keep freedom of choice, are cheap and can overcome bounded self-control (defaults, framing, placement). (b) Case for the view: Nudges keep freedom of choice, are cheap and can overcome bounded self-control (defaults, framing, placement). Case against / evaluation: Effects may be small or temporary; taxes give a reliable price signal and raise revenue; nudges can be manipulative; mix of measures likely best, depending on the scale of the problem. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.
